concepts.title: Isolation of Nucleic Acids from Cells
concepts.definition: Extracting DNA or RNA means rupturing the boundary, shielding the treasure and purifying it: lysozyme digests bacterial walls, SDS or CTAB dissolves membranes while CTAB's ionic strength swaps DNA for polysaccharides, EDTA starves nucleases of divalent ions at mild alkaline pH, chloroform-isoamyl deproteinisation splits phases, and chilled ethanol drops the nucleic acid out of solution - with GITC-phenol-chloroform preferentially pulling RNA into the aqueous phase.
concepts.key_idea: Break the wall, block the nucleases, split the phases and precipitate - four moves that free intact nucleic acid from any cell.
question_patterns: describe the four steps involved in the extraction of nucleic acids
why is CTAB preferred over SDS for isolating DNA from plant cells
what role does the chelating agent EDTA play during DNA extraction
how does guanidinium isothiocyanate help isolate intact RNA from tissues
why are plant cells harder to lyse than animal cells during nucleic acid isolation
how are plasmid DNA and genomic DNA separated by boiling or by alkaline lysis
which solvent precipitates DNA from the aqueous phase and why does it work

solution_steps.explain: Choose lysis by boundary - detergent for animal membranes, lysozyme plus SDS for bacteria, grinding with CTAB for plants.
EDTA chelates divalent cations and alkaline pH plus SDS inhibit DNases and RNases.
Chloroform-isoamyl deproteinisation splits phases; ethanol or isopropanol precipitates the nucleic acid; RNase A clears RNA from DNA prep.

worked_examples.q: Which enzyme digests bacterial cell walls during DNA extraction: lysozyme or ligase?

concepts.title: Restriction Enzymes Types and Cleavage Distances
concepts.definition: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific 4-8 bp recognition sites, mostly palindromic, and fall into three classes: Type I cleaves randomly around a thousand bases away with SAM, magnesium and ATP, Type II cuts precisely within the site needing only magnesium - hence its starring role in cloning - and Type III cuts some twenty-four to twenty-six bases away; names encode the source microbe, genus, species, strain and discovery order as in EcoRI or HindIII.
concepts.key_idea: Only Type II cuts inside its recognition site; compare the cut distances of Types I and III to see how far off-target they work.
question_patterns: Type I enzymes cut about 1000 bp from the site and Type III about 25 bp - how many times farther does Type I cut
why are Type II restriction enzymes the workhorses of rDNA technology
decode the nomenclature of EcoRI and HindIII from their source organisms
what are palindromic recognition sequences and why do most Type II enzymes recognise them
differentiate sticky ends from blunt ends with one enzyme example of each
which cofactors do Type I and Type III enzymes require that Type II does not
whose discovery of restriction enzymes won the 1978 Nobel Prize

solution_steps.explain: Divide the Type I cleavage distance by the Type III distance.
Recognition sites run four to eight bases; six cutters such as EcoRI read six.

worked_examples.q: Which restriction type cuts precisely within its recognition site: Type II or Type I?

concepts.title: Enzyme Toolkit for DNA Manipulation
concepts.definition: Beyond the cutters, cloning borrows a whole enzyme bench: DNA ligase seals 5-phosphate to 3-hydroxyl using ATP or NAD, DNA polymerase extends only from a primer's free 3-OH end, alkaline phosphatase strips terminal phosphates while polynucleotide kinase restores them, terminal transferase adds template-free homopolymer tails, reverse transcriptase copies RNA into cDNA, and poly-A polymerase adenylates RNA ends.
concepts.key_idea: Every joining, filling, tailing and copying job has a dedicated enzyme - match the chemistry to the tool.
question_patterns: write the roles of alkaline phosphatase DNA ligase and terminal transferase in rDNA technology
which energy source do E. coli and T4 DNA ligases each use to seal phosphodiester bonds
why cannot DNA polymerase begin synthesis without a primer
how does reverse transcriptase build cDNA from an RNA template
what are the opposing actions of alkaline phosphatase and polynucleotide kinase
which enzyme adds a homopolymer tail without a template and at which end
differentiate exonuclease from endonuclease action on a polynucleotide chain

solution_steps.explain: Joining needs ligase, filling needs polymerase, tailing needs transferase.
Ligase links a 5-prime phosphate to a 3-prime hydroxyl; phosphatase and kinase add or remove that phosphate.
Polymerases demand primers and templates; terminal transferase and poly-A polymerase work template-free.

worked_examples.q: Which enzyme copies RNA into cDNA: reverse transcriptase or ligase?

concepts.title: Modes of DNA Transfer into Hosts
concepts.definition: Nature moves DNA three ways - transformation by direct uptake, transduction by hitchhiking phage, and conjugation through an F-pilus bridging donor to recipient - and the laboratory extends the menu with calcium chloride heat shock, electric-pulse electroporation, liposome fusion, direct microinjection into the nucleus and gene-gun bombardment of DNA-coated gold particles.
concepts.key_idea: Pick the delivery route by the host - chemical cocktails for bacteria, pores or bullets for stubborn walls and membranes.
question_patterns: differentiate transformation transduction and conjugation as natural modes of DNA transfer
how does the calcium chloride method with heat shock introduce plasmids into bacteria
what creates the transient micropores used in electroporation
why can liposomes fuse with the cell membrane to deliver DNA
which transfer method shoots DNA-coated gold or tungsten particles into cells
what role does the F-factor and its pilus play in bacterial conjugation
name the recipients produced by transformation and by transduction

solution_steps.explain: Free DNA uptake is transformation, virus-borne is transduction, cell-to-cell contact is conjugation.
Chemical (CaCl2, lipofection) or physical (electroporation, microinjection, biolistic) delivery suits different hosts.
Successfully altered recipients are called transformants or transductants.

worked_examples.q: DNA transfer through an F-pilus bridge is called what: conjugation or transduction?

concepts.title: Screening Recombinants by Insertional Inactivation
concepts.definition: Because only a lucky few cells receive the right construct, screening exploits lost functions: direct selection keeps antibiotic-resistant transformants alive, insertional inactivation knocks out a marker gene when the insert lands inside it - tetracycline plates keep all transformants while ampicillin replica plates expose those whose ampR was wrecked - and blue-white screening reads lacZ, where intact enzyme turns X-gal blue and disrupted lacZ leaves recombinant colonies white; GFP offers a fluorescent variant.
concepts.key_idea: Whichever marker the insert breaks tells you which plate or colour hides the recombinant colony.
question_patterns: explain insertional inactivation using a plasmid carrying both ampR and tetR genes
in blue-white screening why do recombinant colonies appear white on X-gal medium
what chromogenic substrate does beta-galactosidase cleave and what pigment results
compare master plate and replica plate colonies to identify recombinant plasmids
how does direct selection with an antibiotic differ from insertional inactivation
how does GFP serve as a screening marker alternative to lacZ

solution_steps.explain: Plate first on the antibiotic whose resistance stays intact - usually tetracycline.
Replica-plate on the second antibiotic or X-gal medium; recombinants fail to grow or stay white.
Colonies present on the master but absent or white on the replica carry the insert.

worked_examples.q: Blue-white screening reads the status of which gene: lacZ or tetR?

concepts.title: Blotting Techniques Southern Northern Western
concepts.definition: Blotting pins molecules onto nitrocellulose, nylon or PVDF membranes for probing: Edwin Southern's capillary transfer finds DNA sequences with labelled probes; northern blotting of 1977 does the same for RNA on charged nylon with formamide buffer; and Burnette's 1981 western runs SDS-PAGE proteins onto membrane and flags the target with a specific antibody - together tracing a gene, its transcript and its protein, with the eastern blot spotting post-translational modifications.
concepts.key_idea: Southern asks about DNA, northern about RNA, western about protein - same membrane logic, different probe.
question_patterns: differentiate the Southern northern and western blotting techniques by their target molecules and probes
describe the capillary setup that transfers DNA from gel to nitrocellulose membrane
why does northern blotting use formamide in the transfer buffer
which membrane type suits northern blotting and why does it favour nucleic acids
who coined the term western blot and in which year
how do the three blots together track a gene its transcript and its protein
what does the eastern blot detect and with which reagents

solution_steps.explain: Restriction-cut DNA, RNA or SDS-PAGE proteins resolve by size on gels.
Capillary flow, electro-transfer or vacuum moves them onto a membrane that is baked or UV-fixed.
Radioactive, fluorescent or chromogenic tags reveal the hybridised or antibody-bound band on film.

worked_examples.q: Which blotting technique asks about RNA: northern or Southern?

concepts.title: PCR Amplification Arithmetic
concepts.definition: Kary Mullis's polymerase chain reaction photocopies DNA exponentially through thermal cycling - strands separate near 95 degrees Celsius, primers anneal around 50-55, and Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus extends at 72 - so the copy count doubles every cycle toward two raised to the cycle number, with real-time qPCR trading gels for SYBR-green fluorescence and Ct values that fall as template rises.
concepts.key_idea: Multiply the starting molecules by two raised to the cycle number; a low Ct betrays abundant template.
question_patterns: starting from 5 template molecules after 30 PCR cycles how many copies are expected
write the expression for the number of amplicons after n cycles of PCR beginning with one template
state the temperatures and purpose of denaturation annealing and extension steps
why is Taq polymerase suited to PCR while human polymerase is not
in real-time qPCR what does a lower Ct value reveal about the sample
how does RT-PCR convert an RNA sample such as SARS-CoV-2 RNA into an amplifiable target
how many cycles does a typical PCR reaction run and how many molecules does one template become

solution_steps.explain: Exponential amplification raises two to the cycle count.
Newly synthesised amplicons are the copies minus the starting templates.

worked_examples.q: Near what temperature do PCR strands separate: 95 degrees Celsius or 55?

concepts.title: Candidate Genes and DNA Libraries
concepts.definition: Finding one 3000-3500 bp gene inside a 3.2 billion base haploid genome is a needle-in-haystack problem, solved by hunting candidate genes tied to disease or agronomic traits and by banking clones: a genomic library houses every fragment of the genome, while a cDNA library made through reverse transcriptase stores only the intron-free transcripts active in a chosen tissue, ready as probes or expression templates.
concepts.key_idea: Divide genome size by gene size to measure the search problem, then let genomic or cDNA libraries shrink it to a shelf.
question_patterns: a 3500 bp gene sits in a 3.2 billion bp genome - how many times larger is the genome than the gene
express the diploid human genome size from the haploid value of 3.2 billion base pairs
differentiate a genomic library from a cDNA library with respect to the sequences each contains
why must mRNA be converted to cDNA before cloning
which enzyme makes the first cDNA strand and which builds the second
how can a cDNA library reveal which genes are active in pancreas beta cells
name two ways to shortlist a candidate gene before cloning

solution_steps.explain: Divide the genome by the gene size to see how many times bigger the haystack is.
Two haploid genomes make one diploid count.
